etymology: Greek kosmios, from kosmos, order or arrangement — well-ordered, seemly, of a piece. The same root gives the English cosmos and cosmetic. Latin modestus, keeping within measure, from modus, a measure.
biblical_def: In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array. The Greek word is kosmios, well-ordered, and the verb Paul uses for adorn is from the same root — a Christian woman is to order herself in ordered dress. The instruction is not primarily about how much cloth is present. Paul's four examples are broided hair, gold, pearls, and costly array, and every one of them concerns expense and display rather than exposure. The context is public worship, and the concern is a woman turning the assembly into an occasion for showing her wealth. That is why he pairs modesty with shamefacedness — a proper reverence and reserve — and sobriety, soundness of mind. Peter makes the same point from the same angle: let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; but let it be the hidden man of the heart. Neither apostle forbids clothing or ornament as such; both relocate the adorning. And Paul finishes the sentence by naming what should be conspicuous instead: which becometh women professing godliness, with good works. The dictionary holds the plain sense — immodesty of exposure is genuinely condemned in Scripture — while insisting that Paul's own emphasis here falls where he put it, on display, expense, and the ordering of a life.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): restrained by a sense of propriety; not forward or bold; not excessive or extreme; moderate; decent.
webster_full: MODEST, a. Properly, restrained by a sense of propriety; hence, not forward or bold; not presumptuous or arrogant; not boastful.
MODEST, a. Not loose; not lewd; as a modest woman.
MODEST, a. Moderate; not excessive or extreme; not extravagant; as a modest request; modest apparel.
SOBRIETY, n. Habitual soberness or temperance; freedom from inordinate passion; calmness; seriousness.
APPAREL, n. Clothing; vesture; garments; dress.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 2:9
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
1 Timothy 2:10
But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works.
1 Peter 3:3
Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel;
1 Peter 3:4
But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
corruption_summary: Modesty is dismissed in the wider culture as an instrument of control, and reduced within the churches to a hemline rule; Paul's word means well-ordered, and his own examples concern display and expense.
corruption_paragraphs: The cultural rejection of modesty treats any standard of dress as an imposition on women and a transfer of responsibility for men's sin. Scripture assigns that responsibility squarely to the man — whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart — and the dictionary does not shift it. But the apostolic instruction still stands, and it is addressed to women as an instruction about their own adorning before God in the assembly. Both things are true at once, and a church that can only say one of them will mislead somebody.

The error inside the churches is to reduce kosmios to a measurement, producing rules about hemlines and necklines that Paul does not give and missing the ones he does. His four examples — broided hair, gold, pearls, costly array — are about conspicuous expense, which means a congregation policing modesty while admiring wealth has inverted the text. The word means well-ordered. It reaches a woman's whole bearing, her speech and her spending as much as her dress, and Paul's positive command is what a watching church should actually notice: good works, becoming women professing godliness.
roots_summary: Greek kosmios (G2887), orderly, well-arranged; kosmeo (G2885), to adorn or set in order; aidos (G127), shamefacedness or reverence; sophrosune (G4997), soundness of mind, sobriety.
roots_lines: Greek kosmios (G2887) — well-ordered, seemly; rendered modest, and of good behaviour of an elder at 1 Timothy 3:2.
Greek kosmeo (G2885) — to arrange, to adorn; the verb rendered adorn, from the same root.
Greek aidos (G127) — a sense of shame, reverence, modesty of bearing; rendered shamefacedness.
Greek sophrosune (G4997) — soundness of mind, self-control; rendered sobriety.
Greek katastole (G2689) — a garment let down, deportment; rendered apparel.
usage: “adorn themselves in modest apparel” — ordered dress, from the word for order.
“not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls” — the examples concern display and expense.
“with good works” — the adorning Paul commands instead.

pos: v. (pilfering; taking small amounts by stealth from a trust)
etymology: Greek nosphizomai, to set apart for oneself, to embezzle — the same verb used of Ananias and Sapphira keeping back part of the price. The English comes through Anglo-French purloigner, to put far off, to remove — and so, to make away with.
biblical_def: Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things. Paul is instructing household servants, and he names the characteristic temptation of a man who handles another's goods daily. Purloining is not robbery; it is pilfering — the small, continual, deniable taking from what one has been trusted with. The Greek nosphizomai means to set something aside for oneself, and Luke uses it of Ananias keeping back part of the price of the land. The offence lies in the trust, not the amount. Against it Paul sets all good fidelity, faithfulness with no reserved portion. Then he gives the reason, and it is the most striking clause in the verse: that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things. The word is kosmeo, to set in order, to make beautiful — the same root as the modest apparel of 1 Timothy 2. A servant's honesty with small things is here called an ornament upon the doctrine of God. Paul says of men at the very bottom of Roman society that their handling of their master's property either beautifies or disfigures the gospel in the eyes of those who watch. Nothing in the passage suggests he thought that a small matter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): stealing; taking by theft, especially in small quantities or by little and little; pilfering.
webster_full: PURLOIN, v.t. To steal; to take or carry away for one's self; hence, to steal in small quantities.
PURLOINING, ppr. Stealing; taking by theft in small parcels; pilfering.
PILFER, v.i. To steal in small quantities; to practise petty theft.
FIDELITY, n. Faithfulness; firm adherence to a person or party with which one is united, or to which one is bound; loyalty; honesty.
ADORN, v.t. To deck or decorate; to make beautiful; to add to beauty by dress; to set off to advantage.
scriptures: Titus 2:10
Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.
Titus 2:9
Exhort servants to be obedient unto their own masters, and to please them well in all things; not answering again;
Ephesians 4:28
Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth.
Titus 2:11
For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,
corruption_summary: Small dishonesty in the handling of an employer's property is widely regarded as a victimless adjustment; Scripture treats it as theft against a trust, and as something that disfigures the doctrine of God.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern conscience has a category for taking a great deal and almost none for taking a little. Time billed but not worked, supplies carried home, expenses padded within tolerance, the small advantage taken where no ledger records it — these are treated as friction rather than fault, and often as compensation for being underpaid. Paul writes to men who genuinely were underpaid, being slaves, and he does not allow the reasoning. The offence is not measured against the wage; it is measured against the trust. Nosphizomai is what Ananias did, and it cost him his life, over a portion of what was his own to begin with.

The more serious loss is what Paul attaches to it. Fidelity in small things adorns the doctrine of God our Saviour. That is a remarkable thing to say about a servant's honesty with the storeroom, and it cuts against the assumption that ordinary work is spiritually neutral ground on which a Christian merely avoids disgrace. A believer's handling of what is not his own is an ornament on the gospel or a stain upon it, seen by people who will never hear a sermon. The doctrine is not made true by his honesty; it is made visible.
roots_summary: Greek nosphizomai (G3557), to set apart for oneself, to embezzle; pistis (G4102), fidelity; kosmeo (G2885), to adorn; didaskalia (G1319), doctrine or teaching.
roots_lines: Greek nosphizomai (G3557) — to put aside for oneself; rendered purloining here and kept back part of Ananias.
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, faithfulness; rendered fidelity, qualified as all good.
Greek kosmeo (G2885) — to set in order, to adorn; what a servant's honesty does to the doctrine.
Greek didaskalia (G1319) — teaching, doctrine; the thing adorned or disfigured.
Greek klepto (G2813) — to steal; the plainer word Paul uses at Ephesians 4:28.
usage: “Not purloining” — pilfering from a trust, not robbery.
“shewing all good fidelity” — faithfulness with no portion reserved.
“adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour” — what small honesty does.

etymology: Greek chalepos, hard, harsh, fierce — used elsewhere in the New Testament only of the two demoniacs who were exceeding fierce. The English comes through Old French perillous, from Latin periculum, danger.
biblical_def: This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. The Greek chalepos is stronger than the English dangerous suggests. It means hard, harsh, savage, and the only other place the New Testament uses it is of the demoniacs of Gadara, who were exceeding fierce. Paul is not predicting difficult circumstances but a fierce moral climate, and he immediately says what makes it fierce. The list is not of wars, plagues, or persecutions; it is of characters: men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy. The peril of the last days is people. And the sharpest clause comes at the end of the catalogue, where Paul places these men inside the visible church: having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof. What makes the times perilous is not opposition from outside but corruption wearing the form of religion, and Paul's instruction is accordingly personal rather than political — from such turn away. He adds a sober trajectory: evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived. And he sets against it the one sufficient resource, in the same chapter: all scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): dangerous; hazardous; full of risk; attended with danger.
webster_full: PERILOUS, a. Dangerous; hazardous; full of risk; as a perilous undertaking.
PERILOUS, a. Attended with danger or risk; as perilous times.
PERIL, n. Danger; risk; hazard; jeopardy; exposure of person or property to injury, loss or destruction.
FIERCE, a. Vehement; violent; furious; savage; ravenous; easily enraged.
GODLINESS, n. Piety; belief in God, with reverence and obedience to his commands; the form of godliness is the appearance without the reality.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 3:1
This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come.
2 Timothy 3:2
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
2 Timothy 3:5
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
2 Timothy 3:13
But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived.
corruption_summary: The verse is routinely read as a forecast of external calamity belonging to a distant generation; Paul describes a moral climate produced by characters inside the church, and he writes of the whole gospel age.
corruption_paragraphs: Dispensational prophecy charts treat the last days as a bounded future period and read 2 Timothy 3:1 as a prediction about the years immediately before a secret rapture — a nineteenth-century scheme, following Darby and Scofield, that no Reformation confession knows. The New Testament's own usage settles the matter: Peter told the crowd at Pentecost that what they saw was what was spoken by the prophet Joel for the last days, and Hebrews says God hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son. The last days began with Christ's first coming. Paul is describing the character of the whole age Timothy was already living in, which is why the instructions that follow are for Timothy now.

The second misreading looks for the peril in the wrong place. Because perilous suggests catastrophe, the verse is used to explain away wars, disasters, and political decline as signs of the end, and a congregation learns to scan headlines. Paul's list is a list of vices, and it ends with men who keep the form of godliness while denying its power. That is a peril the newspapers cannot report, and it is found in pulpits and pews rather than in capitals. His counsel is correspondingly plain: turn away from such, and hold to the Scripture that is able to make thee wise unto salvation.
roots_summary: Greek chalepos (G5467), harsh, fierce, hard to bear; kairos (G2540), a season or times; morphosis (G3446), a form or outline; apotrepo (G665), to turn away from.
roots_lines: Greek chalepos (G5467) — harsh, fierce; used only here and of the exceeding fierce demoniacs at Matthew 8:28.
Greek kairos (G2540) — appointed seasons or times; rendered times.
Greek morphosis (G3446) — an outward form or semblance; rendered form of godliness.
Greek apotrepo (G665) — to turn oneself away from; rendered from such turn away, its only occurrence.
Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed; rendered given by inspiration of God, the resource set against the peril.
usage: “in the last days perilous times shall come” — fierce times, not merely hard ones.
“a form of godliness, but denying the power” — where the peril is located.
“from such turn away” — the instruction, personal and present.

pos: v. (to trip up by the heel; to displace by stratagem)
etymology: Hebrew aqab, to take by the heel, to overreach — the root of the name Jacob. Latin supplantare, from sub, under, and planta, the sole of the foot: to trip a man from beneath.
biblical_def: Take ye heed every one of his neighbour, and trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbour will walk with slanders. The image beneath the word is a wrestler's: to take a man by the heel and bring him down from underneath. Hebrew aqab is the root of the name Jacob, given to the second twin who came out with his hand on his brother's heel, and Hosea recalls the scene — he took his brother by the heel in the womb. Jeremiah uses the word for a society in an advanced state of decay, and the diagnosis is devastating because of where he locates the danger. Not in the invading army, but in the brother and the neighbour. When a people has abandoned the covenant, the first casualty is not its borders but its capacity to trust the man next door. Jeremiah spells out the mechanism in the next verses: they will deceive every one his neighbour, and will not speak the truth: they have taught their tongue to speak lies. Taught is the terrible word — deceit practised until it is fluent. And the prophet names the root rather than stopping at the symptom: through deceit they refuse to know me, saith the LORD. Supplanting is horizontal treachery growing out of a vertical refusal. David felt the same wound from the same quarter: it was not an enemy that reproached me; but it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to trip up the heels; to displace and take the place of; to supersede by stratagem or by unfair means.
webster_full: SUPPLANT, v.t. To trip up the heels.
SUPPLANT, v.t. To remove or displace by stratagem; to displace and take the place of; as, a rival supplants another in the favor of a prince.
SUPPLANT, v.t. To overthrow; to undermine.
SUPPLANTER, n. One that supplants; one that undermines or displaces another by stratagem.
SLANDER, n. A false tale or report maliciously uttered, and tending to injure the reputation of another.
scriptures: Jeremiah 9:4
Take ye heed every one of his neighbour, and trust ye not in any brother: for every brother will utterly supplant, and every neighbour will walk with slanders.
Jeremiah 9:5
And they will deceive every one his neighbour, and will not speak the truth: they have taught their tongue to speak lies, and weary themselves to commit iniquity.
Jeremiah 9:6
Thine habitation is in the midst of deceit; through deceit they refuse to know me, saith the LORD.
Hosea 12:3
He took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God:
corruption_summary: Social collapse is usually explained by structures and conditions; Jeremiah traces the loss of ordinary trust between neighbours to a refusal to know God, and locates the treachery in the brother rather than the stranger.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard modern account of a society that cannot trust itself is structural: institutions have failed, inequality has grown, information has fragmented. Jeremiah 9 gives a different causal order. The lying tongue, the supplanting brother, and the slandering neighbour are all downstream of one thing — through deceit they refuse to know me, saith the LORD. The horizontal ruin follows the vertical refusal. That does not mean structures are nothing; the prophets denounce false balances and bribed judges without embarrassment. It means the biblical categories are covenant, the fallen heart, and national apostasy, and a remedy aimed only at conditions will not reach a tongue that has been taught to lie.

There is a second and gentler evasion available to the church: reading the passage as a description of the world outside, from which the congregation is exempt. Jeremiah was addressing the covenant people, and the terms he uses are brother and neighbour, the words for those nearest. Scripture's hardest warnings about treachery are aimed at the household of faith, because that is where trust is presumed and therefore where its betrayal does the most damage. David's complaint names a guide and an acquaintance, and the Lord himself quoted the psalm of the friend who lifted up his heel.
roots_summary: Hebrew aqab (H6117), to take by the heel, to supplant; Yaaqob (H3290), Jacob, the supplanter; rakil (H7400), a slanderer or talebearer; ramah (H7411), to deceive or beguile.
roots_lines: Hebrew aqab (H6117) — to seize by the heel, to overreach; rendered supplant.
Hebrew Yaaqob (H3290) — Jacob, so named from the heel he grasped; the personal name behind the verb.
Hebrew aqeb (H6119) — the heel itself; the same root that runs through the Jacob narrative.
Hebrew rakil (H7400) — a talebearer, one who goes about slandering; behind walk with slanders.
Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; what the deceitful refuse concerning the LORD.
usage: “every brother will utterly supplant” — the treachery is domestic, not foreign.
“they have taught their tongue to speak lies” — deceit practised into fluency.
“through deceit they refuse to know me” — the root under the symptom.

pos: n. (one who betrays a trust; a betrayer)
etymology: Greek prodotes, from pro, before or forth, and didomi, to give — one who gives another up, a betrayer. Latin traditor, from tradere, to hand over; the same root gives both tradition (what is handed down) and treason (handing over what was entrusted).
biblical_def: And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor. Luke is listing the twelve apostles, and the list ends with a word that must have cost him something to write. Prodotes means one who hands another over, and the horror of it lies entirely in the position the man held. A stranger cannot betray; only a trusted man can. Judas is named among the twelve, sent out with the twelve, trusted with the bag, and present at the table, and the Lord marked the significance of the table when he said, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against him. Judas was no unwilling instrument. Matthew records deliberation and price — from that time he sought opportunity to betray him. Two doctrines meet here and Scripture holds both without apology. The betrayal fulfilled what was written, and the Lord said so plainly: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled. And the betrayer was fully guilty, of whom the Lord said it had been good for that man if he had not been born. Divine decree does not diminish human responsibility, and the clearest case in Scripture of the two standing together is this one. Paul later lists traitors among the marks of the perilous last days, which is to say the character did not end at Gethsemane.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who violates his allegiance and betrays his country; one who betrays his trust; a betrayer.
webster_full: TRAITOR, n. One who violates his allegiance and betrays his country; one guilty of treason.
TRAITOR, n. One who betrays his trust; one who violates his faith or confidence.
TREASON, n. Treachery; a betraying; the highest crime of a civil nature, being a breach of allegiance.
BETRAY, v.t. To deliver into the hands of an enemy by treachery or fraud, in violation of trust.
PERFIDY, n. The act of violating faith, a promise, vow or allegiance; treachery.
scriptures: Luke 6:16
And Judas the brother of James, and Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor.
John 13:18
I speak not of you all: I know whom I have chosen: but that the scripture may be fulfilled, He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me.
Matthew 26:16
And from that time he sought opportunity to betray him.
2 Timothy 3:4
Traitors, heady, highminded, lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God;
corruption_summary: Judas is recast either as a tragic instrument with no real guilt or as a disappointed idealist with a defensible motive; Scripture presents a trusted apostle who sought opportunity and was fully responsible.
corruption_paragraphs: One rehabilitation makes Judas a necessary instrument — if the cross was decreed, the betrayer could not have done otherwise and cannot be blamed. Scripture refuses the inference in the plainest terms available. The Son of man goeth as it is written of him, but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed. Both clauses stand in one sentence, and the second is not softened by the first. The Reformed doctrine of concurrence says exactly this: God ordains what comes to pass, and the creature acts freely according to his own nature and is justly accountable. Joseph's brothers meant it for evil and God meant it for good, and neither verdict cancels the other.

The literary rehabilitation is more recent and more sentimental: Judas as the zealot who wanted to force the Lord's hand, or the only disciple who understood. The Gospels supply no such motive and supply a plainer one. John says he was a thief and had the bag; Matthew records the negotiated price and the seeking of opportunity. The dictionary declines the reconstruction and keeps the text's own emphasis, which falls not on Judas's psychology but on his office. He was numbered with the twelve. That is what makes him a prodotes rather than an enemy, and it is why the warning has always been read as aimed first at those closest to the Lord's work.
roots_summary: Greek prodotes (G4273), a betrayer; paradidomi (G3860), to hand over or deliver up; Hebrew aqeb (H6119), heel, behind lifted up his heel.
roots_lines: Greek prodotes (G4273) — one who gives another up; rendered traitor of Judas and traitors at 2 Timothy 3:4.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to deliver over; the standing verb for the betrayal throughout the Gospels.
Greek dodeka (G1427) — twelve; Judas is repeatedly described as one of the twelve, which is the point.
Greek kleptes (G2812) — a thief; John's verdict on Judas and the bag.
Hebrew aqeb (H6119) — the heel; the psalm the Lord quoted of his familiar friend.
usage: “Judas Iscariot, which also was the traitor” — named in the apostolic list.
“He that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel” — betrayal from the table.
“he sought opportunity to betray him” — deliberation, not compulsion.

pos: n. (one who trains or corrects; a teacher who disciplines)
etymology: Greek paideutes, from paideuo, to train a child — a trainer or corrector, not merely a lecturer. Latin instructor, from instruere, to build in, to furnish, to equip.
biblical_def: An instructor of the foolish, a teacher of babes, which hast the form of knowledge and of the truth in the law. Paul is quoting a Jewish teacher's estimate of himself and letting it run to its full height before knocking it down. The list is impressive and the man believed every word of it: a guide of the blind, a light of them which are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of babes. The Greek behind instructor is paideutes, from the verb used for training and chastening a child, so the claim is not merely to impart information but to form others. And Paul concedes the raw material of the claim — this man really does have the form of knowledge and of the truth in the law; his possession of revelation is genuine. Then comes the question that dismantles the whole structure: thou therefore which teachest another, teachest thou not thyself? thou that preachest a man should not steal, dost thou steal? The indictment is not that his doctrine was wrong but that it stopped short of himself. This is the permanent hazard of every teaching office in the church. A man may hold the truth accurately, train others in it competently, and never once submit to it, and the accuracy will not save him. All scripture is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness — and reproof and correction are listed before instruction.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who instructs; a teacher; a preceptor; one who informs the mind, either by oral address or by writing.
webster_full: INSTRUCTOR, n. One who instructs or teaches; a teacher; a preceptor.
INSTRUCT, v.t. To teach; to inform the mind; to communicate knowledge to.
INSTRUCT, v.t. To direct; to enjoin; to command; to furnish with orders.
PRECEPTOR, n. A teacher; an instructor; the master of a school.
REPROOF, n. Blame expressed to the face; censure for a fault; reprehension.
scriptures: Romans 2:20
An instructor of the foolish, a teacher of babes, which hast the form of knowledge and of the truth in the law.
Romans 2:21
Thou therefore which teachest another, teachest thou not thyself? thou that preachest a man should not steal, dost thou steal?
2 Timothy 3:16
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
2 Timothy 3:5
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away.
corruption_summary: Teaching is widely treated as the transmission of content, so that a teacher's life is held to be a separate question from his competence; Scripture makes the teacher's own submission to the truth part of the office.
corruption_paragraphs: The professionalising of religious instruction has made it possible to separate a man's doctrine from his life and to regard only the first as the church's business. Romans 2 forbids the separation. The man Paul describes has the form of knowledge and the truth in the law, and his teaching may be entirely accurate; the question put to him concerns whether he teaches himself. The apostolic qualifications for eldership are consistent with this — blameless, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, apt to teach — where character and capacity are named in one breath and character occupies most of the list.

A second distortion drains the word itself. Paideutes is a trainer and corrector, from the vocabulary of chastening a child, and Scripture keeps that edge: profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, and then for instruction in righteousness. Where teaching in the church is reduced to information delivery, and correction is felt to be an intrusion on the hearer, the office has been emptied of most of what the New Testament means by it. A congregation that will receive explanation but not reproof has hired lecturers and dismissed its instructors, and the last days are said to be full of exactly such arrangements.
roots_summary: Greek paideutes (G3810), a trainer or corrector; paideuo (G3811), to train or chasten; morphosis (G3446), a form or outline; didaskalos (G1320), a teacher.
roots_lines: Greek paideutes (G3810) — a trainer, a corrector of children; rendered instructor here and corrected us at Hebrews 12:9.
Greek paideuo (G3811) — to train, to chasten; the verb from which the office takes its edge.
Greek didaskalos (G1320) — a teacher; the second term of the boast.
Greek morphosis (G3446) — an outline, a form; rendered the form of knowledge, and used again of a form of godliness.
Greek elegchos (G1650) — proof, conviction, reproof; what Scripture is given for before it instructs.
usage: “an instructor of the foolish” — a trainer, not merely a lecturer.
“teachest thou not thyself?” — the question that dismantles the boast.
“the form of knowledge and of the truth” — genuine possession, stopping short of the man.

pos: n. (a raised platform for reading and preaching)
etymology: Hebrew migdal, a tower or raised stand, from gadal, to be great or lifted up. Latin pulpitum, a scaffold or stage. The Authorized Version's pulpit occurs once, of the wooden platform built for Ezra to read the law from.
biblical_def: And Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose. The one appearance of the word in Scripture is worth the whole doctrine of preaching, because of what surrounds it. The platform was built for the purpose — deliberately, for this use, so the people could see and hear the book. What happened on it is described in the verses following with unusual care. Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people; and when he opened it, all the people stood up. Then: so they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. Three things are named, and they are the anatomy of an exposition. The text is read distinctly, so that the words themselves reach the hearers. The sense is given, so that the meaning is opened rather than replaced. And the people are caused to understand, which makes comprehension the aim rather than impression. The pulpit in Scripture is therefore not a throne but a scaffold — a thing built so that a book can be heard. Its height belongs to the word, not to the man standing on it, which is precisely why the people stood when the book was opened and not when Ezra climbed the stairs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an elevated place or inclosed stage in a church, in which the preacher stands; a desk or stand for a speaker.
webster_full: PULPIT, n. An elevated place or inclosed stage in a church, in which the preacher stands.
PULPIT, n. A desk, or a kind of stage or platform, on which a speaker stands.
PULPIT, a. Pertaining to the pulpit; as pulpit eloquence; pulpit discourses.
DISTINCTLY, adv. With distinctness; not confusedly; without the blending of one part or thing with another; clearly; plainly.
EXPOUND, v.t. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to clear of obscurity; to interpret.
scriptures: Nehemiah 8:4

And Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose; and beside him stood Mattithiah, and Shema, and Anaiah, and Urijah, and Hilkiah, and Maaseiah, on his right hand; and on his left hand, Pedaiah, and Mishael, and Malchiah, and Hashum, and Hashbadana, Zechariah, and Meshullam.
Nehemiah 8:5
And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people; (for he was above all the people;) and when he opened it, all the people stood up:
Nehemiah 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
2 Timothy 3:16
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: The pulpit is treated as a platform for the personality who occupies it, and the reading of Scripture in worship is squeezed out by what surrounds it; Nehemiah 8 makes the platform a servant of the book.
corruption_paragraphs: Where a congregation gathers around a preacher rather than around the Scriptures he opens, the pulpit has changed function without changing shape. The symptoms are familiar: the sermon organised around the speaker's story with the text supplying illustration, the platform redesigned so that nothing about it suggests a book is central, the man's name larger than the church's. Nehemiah's account gives the corrective in a single detail — the people stood when the book was opened. The regulative principle of worship is not fastidiousness about furniture; it is the conviction that God has said how he will be approached, and that what he has appointed is the reading and preaching of his word.

The quieter loss is the public reading itself. Nehemiah 8 makes reading the first act, done distinctly, at length, before anything is explained, and the New Testament keeps the practice — give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine. In many congregations the read portion has shrunk to a verse or two used as a springboard. When that happens the people hear about the Bible more than they hear the Bible, and the giving of the sense loses the thing it was meant to open. A pulpit built for the purpose is wasted on a church that no longer reads the book from it.
roots_summary: Hebrew migdal (H4026), a tower or raised platform; gadal (H1431), to be great, lifted up; parash (H6567), to make distinct; biyn (H995), to cause to understand.
roots_lines: Hebrew migdal (H4026) — a tower, a raised stand; rendered pulpit, its only such rendering.
Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to be great, to lift up; the root of the raised platform.
Hebrew parash (H6567) — to make distinct, to declare plainly; rendered distinctly.
Hebrew biyn (H995) — to discern, to cause to understand; rendered caused them to understand.
Hebrew sekel (H7922) — understanding, sense; behind gave the sense.
usage: “a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose” — built so a book could be heard.
“when he opened it, all the people stood up” — the standing was for the book.
“read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense” — the anatomy of exposition.

pos: adj. (to be feared; worthy of awe)
etymology: Hebrew yare, to fear, to hold in awe. Latin reverendus, the gerundive of revereri, to stand in awe of — literally to be feared, one who must be revered. The Authorized Version uses the word once, and it is used of God.
biblical_def: He sent redemption unto his people: he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend is his name. The single occurrence of reverend in the whole of Scripture is this one, and its subject is the name of God. The Hebrew is yare, the ordinary verb for fearing, and the sense is that God's name is a thing to be held in awe. The psalmist sets it in a sentence about covenant faithfulness: he has sent redemption, he has commanded his covenant for ever, and his name is holy and to be feared. Awe is grounded in what God has done, not in bare power. The next verse draws the conclusion the psalm has been building toward — the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments. That fear is not terror that drives a man away but reverence that begins his wisdom. Isaiah sets the same word against the fear of men, and the contrast is exact: sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. A man will fear something. The question Scripture presses is whether the thing he fears is worth it, and only one name is called holy and reverend.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): worthy of reverence; entitled to respect mingled with fear and affection; a title of respect given to the clergy.
webster_full: REVEREND, a. Worthy of reverence; entitled to respect mingled with fear and affection.
REVEREND, a. A title of respect given to the clergy or ecclesiastics.
REVERENCE, n. Fear mingled with respect and esteem; veneration.
REVERE, v.t. To regard with fear mingled with respect and affection; to venerate; to honor in estimation.
HOLY, a. Properly, whole, entire or perfect, in a moral sense; hence, pure in heart, temper or dispositions; free from sin and sinful affections.
scriptures: Psalm 111:9
He sent redemption unto his people: he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend is his name.
Psalm 111:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever.
Isaiah 8:13
Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.
2 Timothy 3:16
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: A word Scripture uses once, of the name of God, has become a standard honorific for ministers; and the fear of God it names has been widely softened into respect or affection.
corruption_paragraphs: The use of Reverend as a clerical title is not found in Scripture, and the word's one biblical appearance is a description of God's name. The observation has a long Baptist and Puritan pedigree, and it is worth making carefully. The dictionary does not charge every minister who answers to the title with impiety; the usage is ancient in English, largely conventional, and Webster's own 1828 entry records it. But the New Testament is notably sparing with honorifics for ministers — be not ye called Rabbi, the Lord said, for one is your Master — and a church that would not casually attach any other divine description to its officers might ask why it attaches this one. The office is real and honourable; the title is optional, and the word belongs first to God.

The deeper corruption is the softening of the fear itself. Where God is presented chiefly as approachable, reverend becomes a synonym for respected and the awe drops out. Scripture will not permit the reduction. The psalm places the fear of the LORD at the beginning of wisdom, and Isaiah commands that the LORD of hosts be a man's fear and his dread. This is not the terror of the condemned; the same psalm is full of redemption and covenant. It is the creature's proper trembling before a holy God, and its loss is felt everywhere that worship becomes casual and sin becomes small.
roots_summary: Hebrew yare (H3372), to fear, to reverence; qadosh (H6918), holy; berith (H1285), covenant; peduth (H6304), redemption.
roots_lines: Hebrew yare (H3372) — to fear, to stand in awe; rendered reverend here, its only such rendering.
Hebrew qadosh (H6918) — holy, set apart; paired with reverend of the divine name.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; commanded for ever, the ground of the awe.
Hebrew peduth (H6304) — redemption, ransom; what God sent unto his people.
Hebrew yirah (H3374) — fear, reverence; rendered the fear of the LORD in the next verse.
usage: “holy and reverend is his name” — the word's only occurrence, of God.
“the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” — the conclusion drawn.
“let him be your fear, and let him be your dread” — Isaiah, against the fear of men.

pos: n. (a writer or singer of psalms)
etymology: Hebrew zamir, a song or psalm, from zamar, to make music, to strike the strings. The Authorized Version uses psalmist once, in the phrase the sweet psalmist of Israel, spoken of David in his last words.
biblical_def: Now these be the last words of David. David the son of Jesse said, and the man who was raised up on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel, said. Four titles are gathered here at the end of a life, and their order repays attention. He is the son of Jesse — an ordinary man with a named father. He is the one raised up on high — lifted by God, not self-made. He is the anointed of the God of Jacob — a king by divine appointment. And last, when everything else has been said, he is the sweet psalmist of Israel. The songs are named alongside the crown, and it is the songs that the covenant people have carried ever since. David immediately states where they came from: the Spirit of the LORD spake by me, and his word was in my tongue. That single sentence is the doctrine of inspiration in the psalmist's own mouth, and it settles what the Psalter is. These are not religious poems that later generations found useful; they are the word of God given through a man, which is why the New Testament quotes them as Scripture and why the church has always sung them. The office was not David's alone — the Psalter carries Asaph, the sons of Korah, Moses, and Solomon — but the title settles on David, and the church's singing has followed his lead ever since: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a writer or composer of sacred songs; a title particularly applied to David and other authors of the Scriptural psalms.
webster_full: PSALMIST, n. A writer or composer of sacred songs; a title particularly applied to David and the other authors of the scriptural psalms.
PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a composition in verse, designed to be sung in the worship of God.
PSALTER, n. The Book of Psalms; a name given to the collection of psalms of David.
ANOINTED, pp. Smeared or rubbed with oil; consecrated by unction; set apart to an office.
INSPIRATION, n. The infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit; the conveying into the minds of men, ideas, notices or monitions by extraordinary or supernatural influence.
scriptures: 2 Samuel 23:1
Now these be the last words of David. David the son of Jesse said, and the man who was raised up on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel, said,
2 Samuel 23:2
The Spirit of the LORD spake by me, and his word was in my tongue.
Colossians 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Psalm 95:1
O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.
corruption_summary: The Psalms are widely treated as ancient devotional poetry that models honest emotion; David states plainly that the Spirit of the LORD spoke by him, which makes the Psalter revelation and not merely expression.
corruption_paragraphs: The devotional reading now standard in many churches treats the Psalms chiefly as a record of human feeling — useful because the psalmist is raw and unguarded, and therefore permission for the reader to be the same. There is a truth in it; the Psalter does give voice to grief, rage, and confusion without tidying them. But David's own account in his last words is that the Spirit of the LORD spake by him and his word was in his tongue. That makes the Psalms God's speech to his people before they are the people's speech to God, and a psalm of lament is not merely permission to complain but instruction in how a covenant man brings his complaint.

The critical reading damages the same doctrine from the academic side, reassigning the Davidic psalms to later editors and post-exilic communities and treating the superscriptions as devotional fiction. The dictionary holds the Davidic authorship of the psalms ascribed to him, as the New Testament does when it argues from David himself saith. And the practical loss from either direction is the same. A church that no longer regards the Psalter as the Spirit's word will sing less of it, and Paul's command that the word of Christ dwell in us richly, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms, quietly goes unobeyed.

roots_lines: Hebrew zamir (H2158) — a song, a psalm; behind the sweet psalmist of Israel.
Hebrew zamar (H2167) — to strike the strings, to make melody; the root of the psalmist's office.
Hebrew mashiach (H4899) — anointed one; rendered the anointed of the God of Jacob.
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — Spirit, breath; the Spirit of the LORD spake by me.
Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm; commanded for the church's singing at Colossians 3:16.
usage: “the sweet psalmist of Israel” — the last of David's four titles.
“the Spirit of the LORD spake by me” — inspiration, in the psalmist's own words.
“in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” — the church's commanded singing.

pos: v. (to praise; to celebrate with words)
etymology: Greek epaineo, to praise upon, to commend. Latin laudare, to praise, from laus, praise — the root of the English laudable and of the old office of Lauds. The Authorized Version uses the verb once, in a chain of quotations about the Gentiles praising God.
biblical_def: And again, Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles; and laud him, all ye people. Paul is quoting the Psalms, and the quotation is doing heavy doctrinal work in the argument of Romans. He has been proving that Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, and that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy — and he proves it by stacking Old Testament texts in which the nations are summoned to praise Israel's God. The inclusion of the Gentiles is not a late development or a change of plan; it was written into the Psalter and the Prophets from the beginning. Laud is a strong and now nearly lost English word: not to feel grateful but to say so, aloud, publicly. That is what praise is throughout Scripture. It is vocal, corporate, and commanded — O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation. Note that the summons in Paul's quotation is addressed to all ye people, the very nations that had been strangers from the covenants of promise. The vision runs to the end of the book, where a voice out of the throne says, Praise our God, all ye his servants, and ye that fear him, both small and great.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to praise in words alone, or with words and singing; to celebrate; to extol.
webster_full: LAUD, v.t. To praise in words alone, or with words and singing; to celebrate.
LAUD, n. Praise; commendation; honorable mention.
LAUDABLE, a. Praiseworthy; commendable; as laudable motives.
PRAISE, n. Commendation bestowed on a person for his personal virtues or worthy actions; the expression of gratitude for personal favors conferred.
EXTOL, v.t. To raise in words; to elevate by praise; to magnify; to glorify.
scriptures: Romans 15:11
And again, Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles; and laud him, all ye people.
Psalm 117:1
O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people.
Psalm 95:1
O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.
Revelation 19:5
And a voice came out of the throne, saying, Praise our God, all ye his servants, and ye that fear him, both small and great.
corruption_summary: Praise has been narrowed to a musical genre and an emotional state, and privatised into an inward attitude; Scripture commands it as vocal, corporate, and addressed to God by the nations.
corruption_paragraphs: In common church usage praise now names a portion of a service and a style of music, so that a believer may speak of the praise having been good or poor as one speaks of a performance. The vocabulary of Romans 15 runs in a different direction entirely. Praise is a command given to peoples — all ye Gentiles, all ye people — and its content is God and what he has done. When the assessment shifts from the object praised to the experience of praising, the act has turned back on itself, and what is being evaluated is no longer worship.

The opposite reduction makes praise a private disposition: gratitude felt inwardly, with expression optional and corporate expression largely dispensable. Laud stands against it, because the word means to say the praise out loud. Every text in this chain is a summons to open the mouth, and the last vision in Scripture is a voice from the throne calling servants small and great to praise together. The Christian's inward gratitude is real and necessary, but Scripture never leaves it inward, and a faith that never says anything aloud with the congregation has quietly dropped a command.
roots_summary: Greek epaineo (G1867), to praise or commend; aineo (G134), to praise God; Hebrew halal (H1984), to praise or celebrate; shabach (H7623), to laud or commend.
roots_lines: Greek epaineo (G1867) — to praise upon, to commend; rendered laud, its only such rendering.
Greek aineo (G134) — to praise, used of praise directed to God alone.
Hebrew halal (H1984) — to praise, to celebrate; the root of hallelujah.
Hebrew shabach (H7623) — to commend, to laud aloud; the Hebrew nearest the English word.
Hebrew goy (H1471) — nation, Gentile; those summoned to praise Israel's God.

“Praise the Lord, all ye Gentiles” — the nations summoned, as the Psalter foretold.
“both small and great” — the summons at the end of the book.
